crt-tv: The TV. CRT television, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Picture fuzzy? Smack the side of the TV. Still fuzzy? Smack it with feeling. How it works: A beam inside paints the picture one line at a time, super fast. The Real Story: Back then, TVs were big glass boxes with a tube inside that shot tiny beams at the screen to make the picture. That's why they were so deep, so heavy, and why the screen zapped your arm hair. Flat TVs replaced them in the 2000s. Weight: A big one weighed as much as a kid. Back In The Day: It took two grown-ups and one pulled muscle to get it up on the dresser. Saturday mornings started here at 6:58 sharp, two minutes before cartoons, so you could sit through the test pattern like a professional. V-chip: From 2000, new TVs had to let parents block shows. Word On The Playground: Rabbit ears wrapped in tinfoil, angled toward wherever the signal felt like being that day. Touch the screen and every hair on your arm stood up. Turning it off left a little white dot that took forever to die. The static zap: The tube runs on so much power the glass holds a charge.
crt-vcr: The VCR. VCR, 1980s, 90s. Childhood Pro Tip: Set the clock? Absolutely not. Put a piece of electrical tape over the blinking 12:00 and live your life. VHS introduced: 1976, by JVC. The Real Story: The VCR played and recorded VHS tapes. JVC made VHS in 1976, and it beat Sony's Betamax to become the tape everyone used. By the 90s one sat under almost every TV, blinking 12:00. The last ones were made in 2016. Rival format: Sony Betamax, 1975. Back In The Day: The clock on it has blinked 12:00 since the day it came home. We set it to record one episode of Goosebumps and it recorded forty minutes of the weather instead. A T-120 tape holds: 2 hours at SP, about 6 hours at EP/SLP. Word On The Playground: Eats tapes for fun. Knew a pencil-in-the-reel rescue by age eight. The tracking button was basically a slot machine. Late fees from the video store are still technically owed. Last VCRs made: 2016 (Funai) Why 12:00 blinks: The clock resets whenever the power cuts out.
crt-cable: The cable box. Cable box, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Cable box lost signal? Unplug it, count to ten, plug it back in. You are now a cable technician. Channel guide ran on: Old Commodore Amiga computers. The Real Story: The cable box gave your TV dozens of extra channels and unlocked the ones your family paid for. The scrolling channel guide was the Prevue Channel, which ran on old Amiga computers. In 1999 it became the TV Guide Channel. Became: The TV Guide Channel, in 1999. Back In The Day: Somebody always sat on the remote, so the cable box buttons were the real remote. Click through the guide and wait for the Prevue channel to scroll back around to what you wanted. It never did. You watched whatever was on. Fuzzy channels: Paid channels were scrambled unless your family paid. Word On The Playground: The scrambled channels were the forbidden zone. You squinted anyway. Green numbers glowing in the dark all night like a tiny nightlight.
nes: Nintendo Entertainment System. Home console, 1985, Nintendo. Childhood Pro Tip: Game won't load? Blow in the cartridge, push it down, then pray. Repeat until it works or dinner. US launch: October 18, 1985, in New York first. The Real Story: The Nintendo Entertainment System came out in the US in 1985, made to look like a VCR so stores would sell it. With Super Mario Bros., it brought video games back. Blowing in the cartridge never really fixed it. Pushing it back in did. In Japan it was: The Famicom, from 1983. Back In The Day: Step one: blow on the cartridge. Step two: blow on the console. Step three: push it down, hit Power, pray. Step four: the screen flashes, so you blow on it again even though Nintendo said blowing does nothing. It works. It always works. Sold: About 62 million. Word On The Playground: The controller cord was exactly three feet too short. Duck Hunt dog laughed at you and you never forgave him. If somebody hit Reset during a save, a friendship ended. The blinking screen: Worn-out pins in the slot, not dust.
boombox: The boombox. Boombox, 1980s. Childhood Pro Tip: Making a mixtape? Finger on Pause, other finger on Record, breathe only during commercials. Peak era: Late 1970s to early 1990s. The Real Story: A boombox was a big radio with tape decks and speakers you could carry anywhere. Two tape decks meant you could copy tapes and make mixtapes. They ate a lot of batteries, sometimes ten big D batteries at once. Power: Typically 6 to 10 D batteries, or a wall plug. Back In The Day: This thing recorded every Top 40 countdown, each one with the DJ talking over the first ten seconds. Mixtapes were made on it with the patience of a bomb technician: finger on Pause, waiting for the song to start. Dual decks: Made tape-to-tape dubbing easy at home. Word On The Playground: Ate D batteries like a car eats gas. The handle is not designed for shoulders. We used it on shoulders. Cassette format: Compact Cassette, introduced by Philips in 1963.
gameboy: Game Boy. Handheld console, 1989, Nintendo. Childhood Pro Tip: Can't see the screen? Tilt it toward the lamp at exactly 43 degrees and stop breathing. Came out: July 31, 1989, for $89.95. The Real Story: The Game Boy came out in 1989 with Tetris in the box. Nintendo gave it a simple green screen instead of color so four AA batteries would last for hours. With the Game Boy Color, it sold about 118 million. In the box: Tetris. Back In The Day: This Game Boy has survived a drop down the stairs, a long car ride to Grandma's and one full Tetris marathon under the covers, with the worm light clipped on so nobody saw. The screen is green, the batteries are always almost dead, and that is perfect. Screen: Four shades of green-gray. Word On The Playground: Four AA batteries lasted about ten hours, or one road trip. Link cable battles in the backseat. You had to tilt it toward a lamp to see anything. Sold: About 118 million, with the Game Boy Color.
tamagotchi: Tamagotchi. Virtual pet, 1997, Bandai. Childhood Pro Tip: Pet dying during class? Ask to use the bathroom. Stay twenty minutes. Clean up its poop in peace. Released: November 23, 1996 (Japan); May 1, 1997 (US) The Real Story: Tamagotchi was a tiny egg-shaped pet on a keychain. You fed it, cleaned up after it, and if you forgot, it died. It came to the US in 1997 and got banned at a lot of schools. About 98 million have been sold. Creators: Aki Maita and Akihiro Yokoi. Back In The Day: It got confiscated in math class twice. The first one died during a fire drill. This one has been alive for nine days and it poops more than a real dog. Feed it, play with it, clean up after it, and do not, under any circumstances, let it get sick on a school night. Name: Mix of the Japanese 'tamago' (egg) and 'watch' Word On The Playground: Hide it in your sock drawer and it beeps at 3 a.m. to be fed. Pulling the battery tab was the closest thing to opening a present. Somebody always says theirs evolved into the "good one". Sold: About 98.1 million (Bandai Namco, 2025)
bed: The bed. Furniture, Never been made. Childhood Pro Tip: Making your bed is pointless. You're getting back in it tonight. Present this argument calmly. Standard twin size: About 38 by 75 inches. The Real Story: The bed was home base for sleepovers, pillow forts and reading with a flashlight after lights out. Twin beds became the normal kid bed in America. Jumping on the bed was banned in every house, and done in every house. Best uses: Fort foundation, trampoline, under-bed storage. Back In The Day: This bed has hosted every sleepover, every fort, and at least one "it was the dog" situation that is still not discussed. The quilt has been washed so many times the pattern gave up and went psychedelic. Under-bed storage: Usually socks, snacks and one missing library book. Word On The Playground: Monsters live under it. Snacks live under it too, so it evens out. Jumping on it is illegal. Everybody did it anyway. Making it every morning was a rule that lasted three days.
bed-pillow: The smiley pillow. Fair prize, Prize from the fair. Childhood Pro Tip: Missing every ring toss on purpose lowers their guard. Then you still miss. Take the smiley pillow anyway. Smiley designed: 1963, by Harvey Ball. The Real Story: The smiley face was drawn in 1963 by an artist named Harvey Ball. He got paid $45 for it and never owned the rights. It ended up on buttons, shirts and carnival prizes everywhere. Original client: State Mutual Life Assurance Company. Back In The Day: Won it at the fair for three tickets after missing the ring toss eleven times. It has absorbed tears, drool and one whole juice box. Still smiling. Kind of creepy, honestly. Ball's fee: $45. Word On The Playground: Best pillow-fight weapon in the house. Smells faintly of Kool-Aid forever. Trademark: Ball never registered one.
backpack: The backpack. School bag, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Both straps is for nerds. One strap is for legends with a permanent lean to the left. JanSport founded: 1967, Seattle. The Real Story: Backpacks became normal school gear in the 70s and 80s, with brands like JanSport. By the 90s your backpack showed who you were: pins, patches, keychains and your name in marker. One strap or two was a real debate. Common material: Nylon or Cordura fabric. Back In The Day: Wearing both straps was for nerds, so this lived on one shoulder for six years. Inside: a permission slip from 1996, a flattened Lunchable, three pencils with no erasers, and a library book that is now officially stolen. Decor of choice: Pins, patches, keychains and markered names. Word On The Playground: Patches and pins added until it weighed five pounds empty. The zipper broke in October. It stayed broken until June.
beanbag: The bean bag. Furniture, 1968. Childhood Pro Tip: Getting out of a bean bag requires a plan, a grunt, and someone to blame for the noise. Original design: Sacco, 1968. The Real Story: The bean bag chair started as a fancy Italian chair in 1968, a bag full of tiny foam beads that shapes itself around you. Cheaper ones landed in kids' rooms everywhere. Getting out of one gracefully is still impossible. Designers: Piero Gatti, Cesare Paolini, Franco Teodoro. Back In The Day: Sit down and it swallows you whole. Getting out takes two tries and a noise. One seam leaks little foam beads and they were found in the carpet for years. Grab the Game Boy and sink in. Maker: Zanotta (Italy) Word On The Playground: Everybody fought over it during sleepovers. Slowly flattens until you're basically sitting on the floor in a bag. Filling: Expanded polystyrene beads.
window: The window. Window, Grounded view. Childhood Pro Tip: Grounded? Bend one blind slat. Peek. Count how many kids are having fun without you. Mini blind slats: Usually about 1 inch wide. The Real Story: Thin mini blinds were in almost every 80s and 90s house. Summer nights meant a box fan in the window and loud bugs outside. Some cicadas only come out every 13 or 17 years, so some summers were way louder. Periodical cicadas: Come up on 13- or 17-year cycles. Back In The Day: This is the window you stared out of while grounded, listening to everybody else play outside. The blinds have one bent slat where you peeked out to see if the ice cream truck was real. Can-and-string phone: Works only if the string is pulled tight. Word On The Playground: Talked to a friend through a can-and-string phone from here once. It did not work. Summer nights: window open, box fan humming, cicadas screaming.
window-south: The back window. Window, Streetlight side. Childhood Pro Tip: Reading Goosebumps by streetlight counts as bedtime if you're technically lying down. Streetlight type: Orange power-saving lamps. The Real Story: That orange glow outside came from streetlights made to save power. Their orange light made every color look the same at night. Most towns have since switched to bright white LED lights. Replaced by: White LED streetlights. Back In The Day: The streetlight outside turned the whole room orange after midnight. Perfect for reading Goosebumps when you were supposed to be asleep, which made the Goosebumps worse. Word On The Playground: Rain on this window was the best sleep sound ever made.
door: The door. Door, KEEP OUT (this means you) Childhood Pro Tip: A KEEP OUT sign is legally binding for siblings. Parents, unfortunately, have a butter knife. Lock type: Privacy lockset, push-button or turn-button. The Real Story: Bedroom door locks aren't real locks. There's a little hole on the outside so anyone can pop it open with a thin tool in an emergency. That's how every parent got in. KEEP OUT signs were mostly for show. Emergency release: A small hole or slot on the outside knob. Back In The Day: This door has slammed in more arguments than any door in history. Every "you're not the boss of me" ended here. It never locked properly, which was the entire problem. Real effectiveness: Low. Parents always got in. Word On The Playground: Knock first. Nobody knocked first. The lock could be picked with a butter knife. Everybody in the house knew.
door-poster: "I Want to Believe" poster. Poster, 1993. Childhood Pro Tip: Hang the alien poster facing out. That way they know you're on their side. Premiered: September 10, 1993, on Fox. The Real Story: The X-Files started on TV in 1993. Two FBI agents, Mulder and Scully, chased aliens and weird mysteries. Mulder had an 'I Want to Believe' poster with a UFO in his office, and kids everywhere hung one too. Created by: Chris Carter. Back In The Day: Too scared to watch The X-Files, but we still wanted the poster. It stayed on the door so the aliens would know where we stood. Mom thought it was about Jesus. Stars: David Duchovny and Gillian Anderson. Word On The Playground: Stayed up to watch the intro and then hid under the blanket for the rest. Original run: 9 seasons, 1993, 2002. Tagline: The truth is out there.
door-cap: Space Invaders cap. Arcade prize, 1978, Taito. Childhood Pro Tip: Wear the cap backwards. Forwards is for dads and baseball players who aren't cool. Released: 1978 (Japan) The Real Story: Space Invaders came out in 1978 and was one of the first giant video game hits. Rows of aliens march down at you. They speed up as you shoot them because the machine has fewer to draw. That was an accident, and it made the game better. Designer: Tomohiro Nishikado. Back In The Day: Got this from the arcade prize counter for 4,000 tickets. That is roughly 400 rounds of Skee-Ball and one sprained wrist. It hangs on the door because hats indoors were "disrespectful". Publisher: Taito; Midway in the US. Word On The Playground: Worn backwards, obviously. Never washed. Will never be washed. Speed-up: The aliens move faster as fewer remain on screen.
door-pins: The pin collection. Pins, Planet, smiley, alien, star. Childhood Pro Tip: One alien pin equals two Pokémon cards and a pudding cup. Do not let them talk you down. Celluloid button patent: 1896, Whitehead and Hoag. The Real Story: People have collected and traded pins for more than 100 years. In the 90s they went on jean jackets, hats and backpacks. Pin trading is still a big hobby, especially at theme parks. Common types: Pin-back buttons and enamel lapel pins. Back In The Day: Each pin is a trade. The alien cost two Pokémon cards and a pudding cup. The star came free in a cereal box and is probably made of lead. Best display: The backpack, until it rips. Word On The Playground: Pinned to the backpack until the backpack ripped.
nightstand: The nightstand. Furniture, Mission control. Childhood Pro Tip: Candy goes in the back of the drawer. Behind the socks. Under the instructions for the Game Boy. Usual contents: Alarm clock, lamp, contraband candy. The Real Story: The bedside table was mission control: alarm clock, lamp, and a drawer full of things that weren't supposed to be there. Most were cheap wood-look boards, and the drawer stuck unless you lifted it as you pulled. Drawer trick: Lift and pull. Back In The Day: Everything important within arm's reach of the pillow: the alarm clock, the lava lamp, the spare Game Boy, and a drawer of contraband candy that was checked on every night. Typical material: Particleboard with a wood-look finish. Word On The Playground: The drawer sticks unless you lift and pull. Learned that by age five.
ns-clock: Alarm clock. Clock radio, 1990s, RCA. Childhood Pro Tip: Set it seven minutes fast. Then remember it's seven minutes fast. Then snooze seven times. Science. Display: Red seven-segment LED. The Real Story: Red number clock radios sat on every nightstand. Big glowing numbers, a radio, an alarm, and a snooze button as big as the top. When the power blinked, they lost the time, so half the clocks in America flashed 12:00. Snooze buttons: Introduced on alarm clocks in the 1950s. Back In The Day: It's been seven minutes fast since 1994, on purpose, so you'd "have extra time". You knew it was seven minutes fast. You hit snooze seven times. Classic snooze length: About 9 minutes on many models. Word On The Playground: Red numbers you could see from orbit. The power went out once and it blinked 12:00 for a month. After a power cut: Blinks 12:00 until someone sets it.
ns-lava: Lava lamp. Lava lamp, 1963. Childhood Pro Tip: Do not shake the lava lamp. If you shake the lava lamp, do not tell anyone you shook the lava lamp. Invented: 1963, by Edward Craven Walker. The Real Story: A British man named Edward Craven Walker invented the lava lamp in 1963 after seeing a homemade egg timer bubbling in a pub. A bulb warms a blob of wax so it rises, cools and sinks. They came back big in the 90s. First model: The Astro. Back In The Day: Takes forty-five minutes to warm up and in that time you will stare at it for forty-five minutes. Do not shake it. We shook it. It went cloudy and never forgave us. How it works: Heated wax becomes less dense, rises, cools and sinks. Word On The Playground: Swearing you saw a blob shaped exactly like a dinosaur. Too hot to touch, so naturally everybody touched it. Why shaking ruins it: It mixes wax into the liquid and turns it cloudy.
ns-mug: Smiley mug. Mug, Hot cocoa only. Childhood Pro Tip: Correct marshmallow ratio: one cocoa packet, nine marshmallows, zero adult supervision. Recipe: One packet, hot water or milk, stir. The Real Story: Instant hot cocoa packets were made for snow days and after school, with tiny dried marshmallows right in the mix. A mug you made in art class was the official cup. A hard old marshmallow at the bottom was tradition. Marshmallows: Tiny dehydrated ones, already in the mix. Back In The Day: Made in an art class for Mother's Day, then reclaimed when nobody was looking. Holds exactly one packet of Swiss Miss with too many marshmallows. Best served: Snow days and after sledding. Word On The Playground: There's a fossilised marshmallow at the bottom. Leave it.
ns-teddy: Night-shift bear. Teddy bear, 1902. Childhood Pro Tip: Monsters can't get you if a bear is watching the closet. This is a known rule. Look it up. Named after: President Theodore Roosevelt. The Real Story: The teddy bear is named after President Teddy Roosevelt. In 1902 he refused to shoot a tied-up bear on a hunting trip, a newspaper drew a cartoon of it, and a shop owner started selling stuffed 'Teddy's bears.' Origin story: A 1902 hunting trip in Mississippi. Back In The Day: This one stays on the nightstand to keep an eye on the closet door. Has never let a single monster through. Perfect record. Early makers: Morris Michtom (US) and Steiff (Germany) Word On The Playground: Lost an eye in a tug-of-war. Still on duty. Inspired by: A Clifford Berryman newspaper cartoon.
ns-recorder: The blue Sony. Tape recorder, 1980s, Sony. Childhood Pro Tip: Record your own radio show. Then hide the tape forever. Future you will thank you. Cassette format: Compact Cassette, Philips, 1963. The Real Story: Cassette tapes came out in 1963, and small tape recorders let anyone record their voice, the radio or music. Sony even made bright My First Sony recorders for kids. Hearing your own voice played back was a shock. Kids' line: My First Sony, late 1980s. Back In The Day: Recorded songs off the radio, prank calls (allegedly), and a forty-minute "radio show" with your cousin that is still somewhere in a shoebox. Somebody should destroy that tape. Classic trick: Hold Pause, wait for the song, release. Word On The Playground: Hearing your own voice on tape for the first time: horrifying.
ns-yoshi: Yoshi sticker. Sticker, 1990, Nintendo. Childhood Pro Tip: Fastest way to the cereal-box prize: pour the whole box into a mixing bowl. Act natural. Debut: Super Mario World (1990) The Real Story: Yoshi first showed up in Super Mario World, which came with the Super Nintendo in 1991. He's a green dinosaur who eats bad guys with his long tongue and lets Mario ride on his back. Designer: Shigefumi Hino. Back In The Day: Ate a whole box of cereal in two days to get to this sticker. Put it on the drawer the second it came out. It's never coming off. We tried with a butter knife. Signature move: Eating enemies with his tongue. Word On The Playground: Worth the stomach ache. Famous sound: A little 'yoshi!' when you hop on.
ns-tapes: The bedtime stack. Book stack, 1992, 1997. Childhood Pro Tip: Read Goosebumps under the covers. If the flashlight dies, the haunted mask wins. First book: Welcome to Dead House, July 1992. The Real Story: Goosebumps started in 1992 with Welcome to Dead House. R.L. Stine wrote 62 books in the first series, and at its peak it sold about four million copies a month. Every chapter ended on a scary cliffhanger. Original series: 62 books, 1992, 1997. Back In The Day: Bottom shelf, for bedtime only, except it was never bedtime when they came out. Read under the blanket with a flashlight until the batteries died, then you had to lie there in the dark thinking about the haunted mask. Author: R.L. Stine. Word On The Playground: "Reader beware" was not a suggestion. Scholastic book fair day was a national holiday. Cover artist: Tim Jacobus. Tagline: Reader beware, you're in for a scare!
ns-vhs: Movie night tapes. VHS tapes, 1993, 1995. Childhood Pro Tip: Pausing a tape too long chews it up. Pause anyway. The kitchen scene needs studying. Jurassic Park: June 11, 1993, directed by Steven Spielberg. The Real Story: Three movie night favorites. Jurassic Park (1993) mixed robot dinosaurs with computer ones. Hocus Pocus (1993) flopped in theaters and became a Halloween classic on tape. Toy Story (1995) was the first movie made all on computers. Hocus Pocus: July 16, 1993, directed by Kenny Ortega. Back In The Day: Watched every October and most Tuesdays. Hocus Pocus is worn thin right at the part where they sing. Jurassic Park has a little crinkle in the kitchen scene from being paused too many times. Toy Story: November 22, 1995, Pixar. Word On The Playground: Rewind before returning. We never returned these. Toy Story first: First fully computer-animated feature film.
ns-gameboy: Backup Game Boy. Handheld console, 1989, Nintendo. Childhood Pro Tip: Batteries dying mid-boss? Raid the TV remote. Blame the cat. The cat can't argue. Model number: DMG-01. The Real Story: The first Game Boy ran on four AA batteries and was really tough. One got caught in a fire during the 1991 Gulf War and still worked, and Nintendo showed it off in its New York store. Nintendo made Game Boys until 2003. Power: 4 AA batteries. Back In The Day: The spare one, for when the main Game Boy's batteries died at the worst possible moment. Took the batteries out of the TV remote to keep it running. Blamed the remote on the cat. Famous survivor: A fire-damaged Game Boy from the Gulf War that still worked. Word On The Playground: Every house had one TV remote with no batteries in it. This is why. Successor: Game Boy Color, 1998.
south-shelf: The high shelf. Shelf, Display only, do not touch. Childhood Pro Tip: High shelf rule: if a little cousin can reach it, it's no longer yours. Stack accordingly. Purpose: Display only. The Real Story: Every 90s kid had a shelf for the most important stuff: collectibles, the good Game Boy, and toys too old to play with but too loved to give away. Up high, away from little cousins. Threat level: Little cousins. Back In The Day: The good stuff lives up here where little cousins can't reach. Lava lamp, the big teddy, the Game Boy you're not allowed to bring to school, and the View-Master that nobody remembers how to load. Access method: Spinning desk chair (not recommended) Word On The Playground: Needed the desk chair to reach it. The chair spins. That went great.
sh-lava: The other lava lamp. Lava lamp, 1965. Childhood Pro Tip: Lava lamp homework method: check on it every five minutes. Lava done, homework not done. US rights bought: 1965, by Wertheimer and Spector. The Real Story: In 1965 two American businessmen saw the lava lamp at a trade show in Germany and started selling it in the US as the Lava Lite. Lava lamps were huge in the 60s, faded away, then came back big in the 90s. US brand name: Lava Lite. Back In The Day: Birthday present from the aunt who gave everybody lava lamps. This one took a full hour to bloop. Turn it on before homework and check on it every five minutes instead of doing homework. Warm-up time: Usually an hour or more to flow well. Word On The Playground: If the blobs stick at the top, it's too hot. Nobody listened. Blobs stuck at the top: Usually means the lamp is running too hot.
sh-vhs: Home Alone, Jurassic Park, Aladdin. VHS tapes, 1990, 1993. Childhood Pro Tip: Home Alone traps work great on burglars. On dads, less great. Test on a pillow first. Home Alone: November 16, 1990. The Real Story: Home Alone (1990) was one of the biggest comedies ever. Aladdin (1992), with Robin Williams as the Genie, was the top movie of its year. Jurassic Park (1993) was the biggest movie ever made, until Titanic. Aladdin: November 1992; Disney's white clamshell VHS. Back In The Day: Every kid tried a Home Alone trap at least once. Ours was a paint can on a string over the door, and it got Dad. We were not allowed to watch Home Alone for a while after that. Jurassic Park: June 11, 1993. Word On The Playground: "Keep the change, ya filthy animal." The Aladdin tape is the white clamshell one. The good one. 'Keep the change, ya filthy animal': From Angels with Filthy Souls, a fake gangster movie made for Home Alone.
sh-car: Red Hot Wheels. Die-cast car, 1968, Mattel. Childhood Pro Tip: Launching cars off the stairs is science. Write 'experiment' on a piece of paper first to make it official. Launched: 1968. The Real Story: Mattel made Hot Wheels in 1968 to beat Matchbox cars. Their wheels barely touched anything, so they flew down the orange track. The very first one made was a dark blue Camaro. Maker: Mattel. Back In The Day: This one won every race on the orange track loop-de-loop, except when it flew off and hit the dog. It has paint chips from launching it off the stairs, for science. First line: The 'Sweet Sixteen' Word On The Playground: The orange track connectors left marks on everything. Scale: About 1:64. First car produced: Dark blue Custom Camaro.
sh-teddy: Big Ted. Teddy bear, 1902. Childhood Pro Tip: Being too old for teddy bears ends the moment thunder starts. Nobody needs to know. Steiff founded by: Margarete Steiff. The Real Story: In 1903 a German toy company called Steiff brought its teddy bear to a big toy fair, and an American store ordered thousands. That started the teddy bear craze. Real Steiff bears still have a little button in one ear. Big break: Leipzig Toy Fair, 1903. Back In The Day: Big Ted has been through the washing machine four times and a tea party with very strict rules. Retired to the high shelf when you got "too old for teddy bears". He still comes down during thunderstorms. Trademark: The 'Button in Ear' Word On The Playground: The bow tie has been retied by every person in the family. Classic material: Mohair plush.
sh-gameboy: The good Game Boy. Handheld console, 1989, Nintendo. Childhood Pro Tip: Taking the Game Boy to school is fine as long as nobody sees it, hears it, or knows you exist. US release day sales: About 40,000. The Real Story: Game Boys were the thing teachers took away most in the 90s. In the US, 40,000 sold on day one. Pokémon Red and Blue in 1998 kept it going for years after other game systems from its time were gone. Japanese launch: 300,000 units sold out in two weeks. Back In The Day: The one that went to school once, got confiscated, and spent a terrifying weekend in the principal's desk. It lives up here now. Safe. Late-life hit: Pokémon Red and Blue (US, 1998) Word On The Playground: The principal definitely played it over the weekend. Discontinued: 2003.
sh-turtle: Leonardo. Action figure, 1988, Playmates. Childhood Pro Tip: Being Leonardo is fine. Just tell everyone Leonardo is the leader, so technically you're in charge. Created by: Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird, 1984. The Real Story: The Ninja Turtles started as a comic book in 1984. The cartoon came in 1987 and the toys in 1988, and they were some of the best-selling toys of the time. Leonardo wears blue and fights with two swords. Toy line: Playmates Toys, from 1988. Back In The Day: Everybody wanted to be Raphael or Michelangelo, so you got stuck with Leonardo and acted like you didn't care. You cared. Both swords got lost by Christmas. Leonardo's mask: Blue. Word On The Playground: "Cowabunga" was a full answer to any question. Turtle-shaped pizza was technically just pizza. Weapon: Two katanas. Named after: Leonardo da Vinci.
sh-viewmaster: View-Master. Toy viewer, 1939. Childhood Pro Tip: Point it at a lamp for better pictures. Never point it at the sun. Ask someone who tried. Introduced: Around 1939. The Real Story: The View-Master came out around 1939. Each paper reel holds seven pairs of tiny photos, one for each eye, so the pictures pop out in 3D. It started as a travel souvenir and turned into a classic kids' toy. Original company: Sawyer's (Portland, Oregon) Back In The Day: Seven tiny pictures in 3D, and somehow you looked at the same Grand Canyon reel four hundred times. Pointing it at the lamp made it work better. Pointing it at the sun was a mistake. Inventor: William Gruber. Word On The Playground: The orange lever had the most satisfying click in history. Each reel: 7 stereo scenes (14 tiny images)
sh-books: Goosebumps and The Lost World. Books, 1993, 1995. Childhood Pro Tip: Carry the giant book to look smart. Actually read the Goosebumps. Nobody needs the details. The Lost World: 1995, by Michael Crichton. The Real Story: The Lost World (1995) was the sequel to Jurassic Park, and the movie came in 1997. Night of the Living Dummy (1993) was the Goosebumps book that brought us Slappy, the creepy dummy who became the most famous villain in the series. Movie version: 1997, directed by Steven Spielberg. Back In The Day: The Lost World was way too long for a fifth grader but it had a T. rex on the cover, so you carried it around to look smart. Goosebumps you actually read. Twice. Night of the Living Dummy: Goosebumps #7, 1993. Word On The Playground: Night of the Living Dummy ruined ventriloquists forever. Villain introduced: Slappy the Dummy.
toyshelf: The toy cubby. Toy storage, Where everything got thrown at cleanup time. Childhood Pro Tip: Cleaning your room takes ninety seconds if you don't look at what goes in which bin. Method: Throw it in the bin. The Real Story: Cube shelves with bins became the toy storage every kid's room had. 'Clean your room' meant throw everything in the closest bin. Whatever went in there wasn't seen again for months. Average time: Under 90 seconds. Back In The Day: "Clean your room" meant throwing everything into these bins in under ninety seconds. Archaeologists will one day find a Pokémon box, three socks and a single roller skate in here. Contents: A Pokémon box, socks, one roller skate. Word On The Playground: The bins never closed. They were never meant to close.
ts-teddy: Scruffy. Teddy bear, Loved too hard. Childhood Pro Tip: A teddy with no fur on one ear is how you know it's been doing its job. Psychology term: Transitional object. The Real Story: Most kids had one stuffed animal that went everywhere and came back worn out from being loved. Doctors even have a name for it: a comfort object that helps kids feel safe as they grow up. Described by: Donald Winnicott, 1951. Back In The Day: Scruffy went everywhere: the store, the car, the bath, the dog's mouth once. All the fur rubbed off one ear from being held while falling asleep. Common repair: Mom with a needle and thread. Word On The Playground: Mom sewed his arm back on during a sleepover emergency.
ts-handheld: Pocket game. LCD handheld, 1990s, Tiger Electronics. Childhood Pro Tip: There is no volume button. There is only the beep. Parents learn to live with the beep. Company started: 1978. The Real Story: Tiger Electronics made cheap handheld games of everything from Batman to Sonic. Each one played just one game, with pictures already printed on the screen that lit up. Toy maker Hasbro bought Tiger in 1998. Screen: Pictures printed in, they just light up. Back In The Day: One game, one sound effect, no pause button. It came from a birthday party goodie bag and kept everybody busy for a whole car ride. Games per unit: One. Word On The Playground: The beep could not be turned off. Parents tried. Bought by Hasbro: 1998.
ts-clock: Clock radio. Clock radio, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Set the alarm to radio, not buzzer. Waking up to traffic news is worse, but at least it's somebody. Bands: AM and FM. The Real Story: Clock radios put an alarm and a radio in one box by the bed, so you could wake up to music or the morning DJ instead of a buzzer. The radio wire had to be moved around until the station came in. Wake modes: Buzzer or radio. Back In The Day: Set it to the radio instead of the buzzer and woke up to a stranger yelling about traffic. Hit snooze, dreamed about traffic. FM antenna: Often a thin wire you moved until it worked. Word On The Playground: The radio station only came in if the antenna wire touched the window.
ts-skateboard: The RAD skateboard. Skateboard, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Sitting on the skateboard and rolling downhill is a real trick. It's called 'the Survivor.' Origins: California, 1950s. The Real Story: Skateboarding started with California surfers in the 1950s and took off in 1972 when new rubbery wheels gave boards real grip. In 1999 Tony Hawk landed the first 900, two and a half spins in the air, at the X Games. Urethane wheels: Frank Nasworthy, 1972. Back In The Day: Learned exactly one trick: sitting on it and rolling down the driveway. Still a skater. The griptape shredded three pairs of jeans and one knee. First 900: Tony Hawk, X Games, 1999. Word On The Playground: The stickers are worth more than the board. Griptape: Sandpaper-like sheet on the top of the deck.
ts-vhs: Recorded-off-TV tapes. VHS tapes, 1980s, 90s. Childhood Pro Tip: Label every tape. Then tape over it anyway. The label is more of a guess. Key ruling: Sony Corp. v. Universal City Studios, January 1984. The Real Story: Taping shows off TV onto blank VHS tapes was a family hobby, and in 1984 the Supreme Court said it was legal. The slowest speed fit six hours on one tape, but the picture looked worse. Decision: Home 'time-shifting' is fair use. Back In The Day: Half these tapes say one thing on the label and have something completely different on them. The one marked "Lion King" is a Bears game and twenty minutes of a cooking show. Speeds: SP (best), LP, EP/SLP (longest) Word On The Playground: Commercials included, which, honestly, were the best part. Bonus content: The commercials.
ts-lava: Orange lava lamp. Lava lamp, 1992, Mathmos. Childhood Pro Tip: Lava lamps need the whole outlet. Your Game Boy charger can wait. Priorities. Renamed Mathmos: 1992. The Real Story: The company that makes the original lava lamps changed its name to Mathmos in 1992, right as lava lamps got popular again. It still makes them in the same English town where they've been made since 1963. Original company: Crestworth. Back In The Day: This is the tall one that glows like a campfire. Turn the big light off, turn this on, and the whole room looks like the inside of a fruit roll-up. Made in: Poole, Dorset, England. Word On The Playground: It took up the entire desk outlet. Nobody could charge anything. Original 1963 model: The Astro.
ts-pokebox: Pokémon bin. Collectibles, 1998. Childhood Pro Tip: Lent your cousin the Charizard? That's not a loan. That's a goodbye. Pokémon Red/Blue (US): September 28, 1998. The Real Story: Pokémon Red and Blue came to the US in September 1998, right after the cartoon. The cards came a few months later and took over every playground. Lots of schools banned them by the end of 1999 because of trading fights. Original Pokémon: 151. Back In The Day: Card binders, a Pikachu that talks when you squeeze it too hard, and the box the Game Boy Pokémon came in. The Charizard is not in here. Nobody knows where the Charizard went. Ask your cousin. Anime (US debut): September 1998. Word On The Playground: Banned at school by October 1999. Trading card game (US): January 9, 1999.
ts-magazines: Magazine bin. Game magazines, 1988, Nintendo. Childhood Pro Tip: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, B, A, Start. Try it on homework. Didn't work. Nintendo Power first issue: July/August 1988. The Real Story: Nintendo Power came out in 1988 and was where you got maps, tips and cheat codes. The most famous code was up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A, Start, which gave you 30 lives in Contra. Konami Code creator: Kazuhisa Hashimoto. Back In The Day: Game magazines with the cheat codes circled in pen, a poster pulled out of the middle, and an order form for sea-monkeys that we did fill out. Contra code bonus: 30 lives. Word On The Playground: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, B, A, Start. Sea-Monkeys: Brine shrimp, marketed by Harold von Braunhut from 1962.
shelf: The game closet. Board games, 1935, Parker Brothers. Childhood Pro Tip: Monopoly ends one of two ways: bankruptcy or somebody 'accidentally' flipping the board. Monopoly by Parker Brothers: 1935. The Real Story: Monopoly has been sold since 1935. It was based on an older game from 1904 that was made to show why monopolies are bad. Family game night meant Monopoly, Mouse Trap and Sorry!, all of them missing a few pieces. Based on: The Landlord's Game, by Lizzie Magie (patented 1904) Back In The Day: Every family game night started with an argument here about which game, and ended with somebody flipping the Monopoly board. The Christmas lights went up in 1995 and were never taken down. Mouse Trap: 1963, Ideal Toy Company. Word On The Playground: Half the boxes are missing pieces. The other half have pieces from other boxes. Free Parking jackpot: A house rule, not in the official rules.
gs-helmet: Bills helmet. Football helmet, 1990, 1993. Childhood Pro Tip: Tackling the hedges builds character. The hedges will not tackle back, which is the whole appeal. Super Bowls: XXV, XXVI, XXVII, XXVIII. The Real Story: The Buffalo Bills went to four Super Bowls in a row in the early 90s, the only team ever to do it. They lost all four. The first one ended when the winning kick sailed just wide right. Seasons: 1990, 1993. Back In The Day: Four straight Super Bowl trips in the early 90s, and that's all we'll say about that. Wore it in the backyard for every big game and tackled the hedges. Head coach: Marv Levy. Word On The Playground: Football in the yard ended when somebody cried. Usually you. Quarterback: Jim Kelly. Super Bowl XXV: Lost 20, 19 to the Giants after a missed kick, 'wide right'
gs-smiley: Smiley lamp. Lamp, 1970s. Childhood Pro Tip: A smiley lamp is comforting until midnight. After midnight, don't make eye contact. Smiley created: 1963, by Harvey Ball. The Real Story: Harvey Ball drew the yellow smiley face in 1963. In the 70s two brothers added 'Have a nice day' and sold millions of buttons. It came back in the late 80s and 90s on everything, even bedroom lamps. 'Have a nice day' merch: Early 1970s, Bernard and Murray Spain. Back In The Day: A glowing smiley face that stays on all night and stares directly at the bed. Comforting when you're five. Terrifying at eleven. Back to comforting at thirty. Revival: Late 1980s and 1990s rave and pop culture. Word On The Playground: Won it at the fair along with a goldfish that lasted three days.
gs-plant: The plant. Houseplant, Somehow alive. Childhood Pro Tip: The secret to keeping a plant alive is forgetting it exists. Leftover Kool-Aid optional. Hard-to-kill picks: Pothos, snake plant, spider plant. The Real Story: Tough houseplants like pothos and snake plants can live through almost anything, which is why they survive kids' rooms. NASA once tested plants for cleaning the air, but you'd need a jungle to make a real difference. Pothos nickname: Devil's ivy, because it's so hard to kill. Back In The Day: Nobody waters this plant. Nobody has ever watered this plant. It is thriving. Science can't explain it. NASA Clean Air Study: 1989. Word On The Playground: Got the leftover Kool-Aid once. Grew an inch.
gs-lights: The string lights. String lights, 1882. Childhood Pro Tip: One bulb dies, the whole strand dies. Test them one by one. Cancel your Saturday. First electric tree lights: 1882, Edward H. Johnson. The Real Story: The first electric Christmas tree lights were put up in 1882 by a friend of Thomas Edison, with 80 red, white and blue bulbs. On older strands, one dead bulb makes the whole string go dark, so you had to test every bulb. Bulbs on that tree: 80, red, white and blue. Back In The Day: Put up for Christmas 1995 and never taken down, because the room just looked better. One bulb goes out and you have to test every single bulb on the strand. It took an entire Saturday. Series wiring: One bad bulb can kill the whole strand. Word On The Playground: Unplug them at night or they "start fires" (they never started fires). Modern fix: Shunts let current pass a dead bulb.
dresser: The dresser. Furniture, Sticker museum. Childhood Pro Tip: Stickers on furniture are illegal. Unless they're Nintendo stickers. Then they're art. Bottom drawer: Clothes. The Real Story: The dresser kept clothes in the bottom drawers and secrets in the top one. In a lot of 90s houses it was also covered in stickers from magazines, cereal boxes and the book fair. Those stickers never come all the way off. Top drawer: Anything important. Back In The Day: Nobody was allowed to put stickers on the furniture. We put stickers on the furniture. Now the dresser is basically a history book: Mario, Yoshi, No Fear, and a smiley face that won't come off. Sticker removal: Hair dryer heat helps; patience mostly doesn't. Word On The Playground: Bottom drawer: clothes. Top drawer: anything important.
dr-stickers: Mario and Yoshi stickers. Stickers, 1988, Nintendo. Childhood Pro Tip: Peeling a sticker halfway is the worst choice. Commit. Leave it or lose it forever. Mario's debut: Donkey Kong (1981), as 'Jumpman' The Real Story: Mario first showed up in Donkey Kong in 1981, where he was called Jumpman. By the 90s Nintendo characters were on everything, and Nintendo Power came with posters and stickers. The magazine ran until 2012. Created by: Shigeru Miyamoto. Back In The Day: They came free in a magazine and went straight onto the dresser before anybody could stop it. They've survived three moves and one aggressive scrubbing. Nintendo Power run: 1988, 2012. Word On The Playground: Peeling one off halfway and then putting it back was worse than leaving it. Yoshi's debut: Super Mario World (1990)
dr-nofear: No Fear sticker. Sticker, 1989. Childhood Pro Tip: No Fear means no fear. Except of Mom finding the sticker on the dresser. That's normal fear. Founded: 1989. The Real Story: No Fear started in 1989 in Southern California, from the dirt bike racing crowd. Its shirts had big tough sayings about winning, and by the mid-90s the logo was everywhere: shirts, stickers and car windows. Founders: Mark Simo, Brian Simo, Marty Moates. Back In The Day: No Fear shirts had sayings like "Second place is the first loser". We thought that was deep. Put this sticker on the dresser and immediately got scared of getting caught. Roots: Motocross and racing. Word On The Playground: Fear: medium. Known for: Slogan T-shirts and stickers.
clutterdesk: The homework desk. Desk, Homework was never done here. Childhood Pro Tip: Homework done on the bus counts the same. The bus is just a moving desk. Modern LEGO brick: Patented 1958. The Real Story: The desk was for homework, officially. Really it was for LEGO, drawing, snacks and games. The LEGO brick we know came out in 1958, and by the 90s every desk drawer had a few loose ones. LEGO founded: 1932, by Ole Kirk Christiansen, Denmark. Back In The Day: This desk was for homework. It was used for building Lego, drawing, eating pizza rolls, playing Super Nintendo with the sound off, and hiding the report card. Homework happened on the bus. Name: From Danish 'leg godt,' meaning 'play well' Word On The Playground: Every drawer is a junk drawer. The stickers are load-bearing.
cd-lava: Desk lava lamp. Lava lamp, 1963. Childhood Pro Tip: Never put crayons next to the lava lamp. Unless you want a new crayon shaped like a puddle. Heat comes from: A light bulb in the base. The Real Story: A lava lamp is just a bulb under a bottle of liquid and wax. The heat makes the wax rise, it cools off at the top, and it sinks again, over and over. The base gets really hot, so don't touch it. Idea came from: An egg timer bubbling on a stove. Back In The Day: Turned on "to help focus". Spent the next hour naming the blobs. That one's Gary. Gary just split into two Garys. The base gets: Hot. Very hot. Word On The Playground: Do not put your crayons next to it. Learned that the waxy way.
cd-cup: Smiley pencil cup. Pencil cup, Full of pens that don't work. Childhood Pro Tip: Every dead pen goes back in the cup. Someday one will work again. Hope is free. Gel pen invented: 1984, Sakura Color Products. The Real Story: Gel pens were invented in Japan in 1984, and the glitter, milky and scented ones were all over 90s schools. Clicky pens are older: Parker's Jotter came out in 1954. Somebody always borrowed your best one. Famous line: Gelly Roll. Back In The Day: Twenty pens in here and not one writes. Somehow you keep putting dead pens back in. There's a gel pen at the bottom that smells like grapes. Parker Jotter: 1954. Word On The Playground: Click pens: clicked eight thousand times during tests. 90s favorites: Glitter, milky and scented inks.
cd-tapes: Video game tape stack. Rental tapes, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Return the rental before it's due. Or don't, and owe the store a car payment. Blockbuster founded: 1985, Dallas, Texas. The Real Story: You rented movies and video games from the video store, and Blockbuster was the biggest one. It started in 1985 and had about 9,000 stores by 2004, then streaming took over. One store is still open, in Bend, Oregon. Founder: David Cook. Back In The Day: A stack from the rental store, a couple of them still in their own cases with the store's sticker. The late fee is now worth more than the store. Peak: About 9,000 stores (2004) Word On The Playground: Blockbuster night was a Friday-night ritual. Last store: Bend, Oregon. Most feared phrase: Late fee.
cd-car: Red sports car. Die-cast car, 1953. Childhood Pro Tip: Car noises must be made with your mouth. The louder the noise, the faster the car. Facts. Matchbox launched: 1953, by Lesney Products (UK) The Real Story: Tiny metal toy cars took off in 1953 when a man made one small enough to fit in a matchbox for his daughter, and Matchbox was born. Mattel answered with Hot Wheels in 1968. Hot Wheels launched: 1968, by Mattel. Back In The Day: Somebody's going to buy this car for real one day. Somebody being you. Until then it lives next to the lava lamp, doing laps around the pencil cup. Common scale: About 1:64. Word On The Playground: Engine noises: done with your mouth, very loud.
cd-clock: Clock radio. Clock radio, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Don't know how to change the alarm? Leave it. You're now an early riser. Congratulations. Common snooze: About 9 minutes. The Real Story: Clock radios had an alarm, a clock and a radio, with a big snooze button for slapping in the dark. Snooze usually gave you nine more minutes. Setting the time meant holding a button while the numbers raced by. Display: Red LED digits. Back In The Day: The alarm was set for paper-route time once, as a business venture. The business lasted a week. The alarm stayed at 5:41 for another year because nobody knew how to change it. Setting it: Hold a button while the numbers race by. Word On The Playground: Hitting the snooze button blind in the dark is a skill.
cd-phone: Brick phone. Cell phone, 1983. Childhood Pro Tip: Snake isn't a game. It's 'checking if the phone still works.' For twenty minutes. First handheld cell phone: Motorola DynaTAC 8000X, 1983. The Real Story: The first cell phone you could buy came out in 1983, cost $3,995, and was so big people called it 'the brick.' Phones got much smaller in the 90s, and in 1997 Nokia added Snake, one of the first famous phone games. Launch price: $3,995. Back In The Day: Mom's old phone, "only for emergencies". Every time it was used was not an emergency. Twenty minutes of Snake counts as a call to grandma, right? Snake debut: Nokia 6110, 1997. Word On The Playground: Ringtone: composed yourself, note by note, one awful afternoon. Snake creator: Taneli Armanto.
cd-pogs: POGs. Milk caps, Early 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Never play for keeps. If you do play for keeps, bring the skull slammer and no feelings. Name comes from: POG juice: Passion fruit, Orange, Guava. The Real Story: POG was a juice from Hawaii: Passion fruit, Orange and Guava. A teacher there brought back an old game of flipping the bottle caps in 1991, and by the mid-90s every school had it. Stack the caps, throw the slammer, keep what flips. Juice created: 1971, by Mary Soon for Haleakala Dairy. Back In The Day: POGs got banned at school because a kid lost his whole collection playing "for keeps" and cried in the nurse's office. The heavy slammer on top is the one that won all these. Game revived: 1991, Hawaii. Word On The Playground: The skull slammer was the most powerful object in the cafeteria. Named after a juice. Nobody drank the juice. Peak craze: Early to mid-1990s. Slammer: A heavier cap, often plastic or metal.
cd-sketch: The sketchbook (and the Cool S) Doodle, Graffiti letters, every page. Childhood Pro Tip: Drawing the Cool S is easy. Six lines, then six more, then connect. Takes a lifetime to master. Also called: Stussy S, Superman S, Pointy S. The Real Story: The 'Cool S' was drawn on every notebook in every school, and nobody knows who started it. It's made from two rows of three lines, which is why so many kids figured it out on their own. Inventor: Unknown. Back In The Day: Every page is the same cool S, over and over, plus a dragon that doesn't look like a dragon. Everyone drew the S. Nobody knows who invented the S. Construction: Two rows of three parallel lines, then connect. Word On The Playground: Drew in the margins of every worksheet too. Back page: fake signatures, practicing for the report card.
cd-lamp: Desk lamp. Desk lamp, Burns fingers on contact. Childhood Pro Tip: Old desk lamps double as interrogation lights. Point it at your little brother. Ask where the remote went. Incandescent waste: About 90% of energy becomes heat. The Real Story: Old light bulbs turned most of their power into heat instead of light, which is why desk lamps burned your fingers. The bendy desk lamp design comes from the 1930s. Cooler LED bulbs have mostly taken over. Balanced-arm lamp: Anglepoise, George Carwardine, 1930s. Back In The Day: The bulb got so hot you could warm up a Hot Pocket on it. We did not try that. Okay, we tried that. Replaced by: Compact fluorescents, then LEDs. Word On The Playground: Pointed at your face during "interrogations" with your little brother.
cd-frog: Little green guy. Meal toy, 1979. Childhood Pro Tip: The toy is the meal. The food is just packaging. Every kid knows this. Happy Meal launched: 1979, nationwide in the US. The Real Story: McDonald's started the Happy Meal across the US in 1979, and the toy inside became the real reason kids wanted one. Burger King and others followed. The biggest 90s toy craze was Teenie Beanie Babies in 1997. Biggest 90s craze: Teenie Beanie Babies, 1997. Back In The Day: Came free with a kid's meal. Worth more than the meal. He's been the desk lamp's security guard ever since. Value: Higher than the meal, emotionally. Word On The Playground: Had a name once. Nobody remembers it.
cd-8ball: Magic 8 Ball. Fortune toy, 1950. Childhood Pro Tip: If the Magic 8 Ball says no, shake it again. Keep shaking until it agrees. That's how science works. Came out: Around 1950. The Real Story: The Magic 8 Ball came out around 1950. Shake it, flip it, and a floating answer shows up in the window. Inside is a 20-sided shape in blue liquid with 10 yes answers, 5 no answers and 5 maybes. Inside: A 20-sided shape floating in blue liquid. Back In The Day: Asked it if you'd pass the spelling test. It said "Outlook not so good". It was right. Asked it if your crush liked you back. It said "Ask again later". It's been later for a long time. Answers: 10 yes, 5 maybe, 5 no. Word On The Playground: Shook it until it gave you the answer you wanted. Owned by: Mattel.
cd-photo: The photo. School photo, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Practice your smile in the mirror for a week. Blink right as the flash goes off. Lifetouch founded: 1936. The Real Story: Picture day meant a laser background, a free plastic comb, and tiny wallet photos to trade with friends. Companies like Lifetouch took millions of school pictures every year. Retake day was a second chance that rarely helped. 90s look: Laser backgrounds. Back In The Day: School picture day: laser background, a comb the photographer used on everyone, and a smile you practiced in the mirror. Ordered the wallet sizes, gave them to everybody. Package staple: Wallet-size prints. Word On The Playground: The retake was somehow worse. Free gift: A plastic comb.
cd-tmnt: Ninja Turtles cup. Cup, 1990. Childhood Pro Tip: A pizza place cup holds markers forever. It also holds the smell of Sprite forever. Fair trade. First movie: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, March 1990. The Real Story: Turtle mania was huge: the cartoon started in 1987 and the first live-action movie came out in 1990, with turtle suits made by Jim Henson's team. Turtles were on cups, cereal and toys, and pizza places loved them. Turtle suits: Jim Henson's Creature Shop. Back In The Day: This cup came with a large pizza and a toy that broke in the car. It holds markers now. Smells faintly of Sprite and a little like pizza. Movie theme: 'Turtle Power!' by Partners in Kryme. Word On The Playground: Turtle Power. Favorite food: Pizza.
cd-walkman: Walkman. Cassette player, 1979, Sony. Childhood Pro Tip: Save batteries: rewind tapes with a pencil. Spin it fast. Your wrist will survive. First model: TPS-L2, July 1, 1979. The Real Story: Sony's first Walkman came out in 1979 and let you carry your music anywhere. Later ones could flip the tape for you, called auto-reverse. Sony sold about 220 million tape Walkmans before stopping in 2010. Auto-reverse: Added in 1982. Back In The Day: Bus rides were a whole movie with this on. The foam earpieces were orange once. Now they're a color science doesn't have a name for. Auto-reverse was basically magic. Cassette Walkmans sold: About 220 million. Word On The Playground: Rewinding a tape with a pencil to save batteries. The tape got eaten right at the best part. Every time. Cassette production ended: 2010 (Japan)
cd-snes: Donkey Kong Country cartridge. SNES game, 1994, Rare. Childhood Pro Tip: If it doesn't work, just blow in it. Nothing says advanced troubleshooting like a little 90s spit. Came out: November 1994. The Real Story: Donkey Kong Country came out for the Super Nintendo in 1994. The team built the characters on powerful computers first, so the game looked way better than anything else on the system. It sold over 9 million copies. Made by: Rare, a game studio in England. Back In The Day: Christmas morning 1994. Unwrapped, plugged in, played until the TV got hot. The minecart levels made grown men throw controllers. This cartridge has seen things. The look: Built as 3D models first, then turned into game art. Word On The Playground: Blowing on SNES carts did nothing either. We did it anyway. Sold: 9.3 million copies.
cd-yoyo: Yo-yo. Yo-yo, 1929, Duncan. Childhood Pro Tip: Practice 'walk the dog' away from the dog. Practice 'around the world' away from the lamp. So, outside. Pedro Flores Yo-yo Company: 1928, Santa Barbara. The Real Story: Yo-yos took off in America in the 1920s and 30s when Duncan sent yo-yo pros to schools to show off tricks and run contests. The 90s had its own yo-yo craze, done the same way. Duncan: Took over in the early 1930s. Back In The Day: "Walk the dog" actually hit the dog. "Around the world" hit the lamp. "Rock the baby" got the string tangled into a knot that's still in there. Classic tricks: Walk the Dog, Around the World, Rock the Baby. Word On The Playground: The yo-yo guy came to school and everybody bought one that afternoon. Marketing secret: Touring yo-yo demonstrators.
cd-sonic: Sonic tape. VHS tape, 1991, Sega. Childhood Pro Tip: Sonic or Mario? Say 'both' and you'll be fine. Say 'Mario' at the wrong lunch table and you won't. Game released: June 23, 1991 (Genesis) The Real Story: Sega made Sonic the Hedgehog in 1991 to take on Mario. Two Sonic cartoons came out in 1993: a silly one where he loved chili dogs, and a more serious Saturday morning one. Creators: Yuji Naka and Naoto Ohshima. Back In The Day: The Sonic cartoon taped off Saturday morning TV. Sonic vs Mario was the real war of the 90s, and this desk was Switzerland: both of them lived here. Cartoons: Two Sonic series debuted in 1993. Word On The Playground: Chili dogs became the only acceptable food for a month. Favorite food: Chili dogs. Rival: Mario.
cd-vhs: The movie row. VHS tape, 1996, Warner Bros. Childhood Pro Tip: To dunk like Michael Jordan, lower the hoop to four feet. Then tell everyone it was regulation. Released: November 15, 1996. The Real Story: Space Jam (1996) put Michael Jordan on a basketball team with Bugs Bunny and the Looney Tunes against aliens called the Monstars. It was the number one movie when it came out, and the soundtrack was everywhere. Director: Joe Pytka. Back In The Day: Space Jam came out and everybody tried to dunk like Michael Jordan on the mini hoop on the closet door. Monstars were the scariest villains ever made, change my mind. Stars: Michael Jordan and the Looney Tunes. Word On The Playground: The Space Jam soundtrack lived in the Walkman for a year. Worldwide gross: About $250 million. Villains: The Monstars.
cd-trophy: Participation trophy. Trophy, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Losing every game still gets a trophy. Keep losing with confidence. The trophy doesn't know. Tee-ball ages: Usually about 4 to 7. The Real Story: Tee-ball, where you hit the ball off a stand instead of a pitch, was the first sport for a lot of little kids. Many leagues gave every player a trophy at the end of the season, win or lose. Trophy style: Gold-colored plastic figure on a base. Back In The Day: Tee-ball, 1995. The team lost every single game and everybody got a trophy anyway. It's gold-colored plastic and it is the proudest thing on this desk. Best part of the game: Orange slices. Word On The Playground: Orange slices at halftime were the actual reason anybody played.
cd-stickers: Drawer stickers. Stickers, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Charge glow-in-the-dark stickers with a flashlight right before bed. Then immediately fall asleep and miss it. Old glow stickers: Faded in a few minutes. The Real Story: Glow-in-the-dark stickers soak up light and slowly give it back in the dark. Older ones faded fast. New ones from the 90s glowed brighter and much longer. Skater and surf stickers were a whole other collection. 90s glow stickers: Glowed bright for much longer. Back In The Day: Every drawer has a sticker from a different phase: the skater phase, the space phase, the No Fear phase. The drawers are a timeline of who you were trying to be. Charge them with: Any bright light. Word On The Playground: The planet sticker glows in the dark if the lights were on long enough.
cd-chair: The spinny chair. Desk chair, Mission control. Childhood Pro Tip: Spin until dizzy. Spin back the other way to cancel it out. This does not work. Spin anyway. Early swivel chair: Credited to Thomas Jefferson, 1776. The Real Story: Thomas Jefferson is said to have used a spinning chair while writing the Declaration of Independence. Rolling desk chairs became normal in offices later, and kids found out they're perfect for hallway races. Wheels pioneer: Charles Darwin (by legend) Back In The Day: Its main job: spin until you feel sick, then spin back the other way to "unwind". The cushion has a hole that grows a little every year.
